questions.question: Operation Flood is related to which of the following?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dairy industry of India**__.

__
 
• **Operation Flood** was a landmark project initiated by the **National Dairy Development Board (NDDB)** in **1970**, designed to increase milk production in India and transform the country into one of the largest producers of milk globally.
 
• It is often referred to as the **"White Revolution"** in India due to its significant role in boosting dairy farming and milk production.
 
• The initiative was spearheaded by **Dr. Verghese Kurien**, regarded as the "Father of the White Revolution."
 
• The program focused on establishing a nationwide milk grid, ensuring the availability of milk and dairy products even in remote areas, while eliminating dependence on imports.
 
• Operation Flood not only improved milk production but also enhanced the economic conditions of millions of rural farmers and dairy producers across India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Key Objectives of Operation Flood:**

 
 
• To create a nationwide milk grid for uninterrupted milk supply throughout the year.
 
• To increase self-sufficiency in milk production by reducing reliance on imports.
 
• To support rural development by providing income opportunities to farmers, especially small-scale producers.
 
• To improve nutrition levels by ensuring availability of milk and dairy products at affordable prices.
 
 
 
• **Phases of Operation Flood:**
 
 
• **Phase I (1970-1980):** Focused on building dairy infrastructure and establishing milk grids in major cities.
 
• **Phase II (1981-1985):** Expanded the milk grid to include more cities and regions, boosting production and marketing.
 
• **Phase III (1985-1996):** Consolidated the achievements and expanded the milk grid nationwide, ensuring sustainability.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Rural Economy:**
 
 
• Empowered rural farmers, particularly women, by providing stable income sources through dairy farming.
 
• Created employment opportunities in milk production, processing, and distribution sectors.
 
• Helped alleviate poverty in rural areas and improved the standard of living.
 
 
 
• **India's Global Position:**
 
 
• Operation Flood made India the **largest producer of milk globally**, surpassing countries like the USA and New Zealand.
 
• The dairy sector contributes significantly to India's agricultural GDP, accounting for around **4% of the national GDP**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Verghese Kurien:**

 
 
• Known as the **"Father of the White Revolution"**, Dr. Kurien played a pivotal role in transforming India's dairy industry.
 
• He was instrumental in the establishment of the **Amul cooperative** and the success of Operation Flood.
 
• He was honored with numerous awards, including the **Padma Vibhushan** for his contributions to the dairy sector.
 
 
 
• **Challenges Faced:**
 
 
• Initially, there was resistance from traditional dairy producers to adopt modern farming practices.
 
• Infrastructure limitations, such as cold storage and transportation facilities, posed challenges.
 
• Efforts were made to educate rural farmers on improved breeding, feeding, and veterinary practices.
 
 
 
• **Current Status:**
 
 
• India remains the **largest producer of milk**, contributing significantly to global dairy production.
 
• The dairy industry continues to play a vital role in the country's economy and rural development.

questions.question: Which of the following is a matter included in the State List in the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Markets and fairs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **State List in the Seventh Schedule:** The **Indian Constitution** divides powers between the Union and State governments under three lists: Union List, State List, and Concurrent List. The State List contains subjects on which states have exclusive legislative powers.
 
• **Markets and fairs:** This subject is explicitly included in the **State List** under Entry 28 of the Seventh Schedule, empowering states to regulate and manage markets and fairs within their territories.
 
• **Extradition:** Extradition falls under the **Union List** (Entry 18), as it deals with international matters and requires central authority coordination. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **War and peace:** Matters related to war and peace are included in the **Union List** (Entry 1), as they pertain to national security and foreign relations. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Railway:** Railways are a subject of the **Union List** (Entry 22), reflecting their significance as a national infrastructure. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*
 
• **Correct Option:** Markets and fairs are managed by state governments, as specified under the State List. *Hence, the correct answer is **Markets and fairs**.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution:**
 
 
• The Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution outlines the division of subjects between the Union and State governments through three lists: Union List, State List, and Concurrent List.
 
• The **Union List** contains 97 subjects such as defense, foreign affairs, and atomic energy, where only the Union government can legislate.
 
• The **State List** includes 66 subjects like police, public health, and agriculture, allowing states to have exclusive legislative powers.
 
• The **Concurrent List** comprises 47 subjects such as education, marriage, and adoption, where both Union and State governments can legislate, but Union law prevails in case of conflict.
 
 
 
• **Key subjects under the State List:**
 
 
• Important subjects include **markets and fairs, police, public health, agriculture, irrigation, and local government.**
 
• State governments have the authority to regulate these subjects independently within their territories.
 
 
 
• **Union List subjects:**
 
 
• Subjects like **defense, foreign affairs, railways, extradition, and war and peace** fall under the Union List, requiring centralized control due to their national and international significance.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List subjects:**
 
 
• Subjects like **education, marriage, adoption, and forests** require joint efforts from both Union and State governments.
 
• Union legislation overrides state legislation if conflicts arise.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• The division of subjects between lists ensures a clear framework for governance and minimizes conflicts between the Union and State governments.
 
• Any changes to the lists require a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
 
• The system reflects India's federal structure, balancing autonomy and unity.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases is caused due to deficiency of protein?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Kwashiorkor**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kwashiorkor** is a severe form of malnutrition caused due to **protein deficiency** in the diet. It is most commonly seen in children in developing countries.
 
• This condition occurs when the intake of **protein** is insufficient, although the caloric intake may be adequate, leading to symptoms such as **edema**, irritability, and an enlarged fatty liver.
 
• The disease is characterized by symptoms such as **swelling in the abdomen and legs**, reddish discoloration of hair, failure to grow, and mental changes like apathy.
 
• **Kwashiorkor** is more common in regions where famine, limited food supply, or low levels of education about nutrition exist.
 
• The treatment involves introducing a balanced diet rich in **proteins, vitamins, and minerals**, along with medical supervision.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Bronchitis:**

 
 
• **Bronchitis** is a respiratory disease involving the inflammation of the bronchial tubes. It is not caused by a lack of protein but is often triggered by **viral infections** or exposure to irritants like **tobacco smoke**.
 
• Symptoms include **persistent coughing, shortness of breath**, and chest discomfort.
 
• Treatment involves rest, hydration, and in some cases, bronchodilators or antibiotics.
 
 
 
• **Anaemia:**
 
 
• **Anaemia** is commonly caused by a deficiency of **iron**, vitamin B12, or folic acid rather than protein.
 
• The condition leads to a decreased number of red blood cells or hemoglobin in the blood, causing symptoms like **fatigue, weakness**, and pale skin.
 
• Treatment generally involves iron supplements and dietary modifications.
 
 
 
• **Goitre:**
 
 
• **Goitre** is caused by an **iodine deficiency** in the diet, leading to abnormal enlargement of the thyroid gland.
 
• Symptoms may include swelling in the neck and difficulty swallowing or breathing.
 
• The condition is treated by increasing iodine intake through iodized salt or supplements.
 
 
 
• **Protein Deficiency Diseases:**
 
 
• Other diseases related to protein deficiency include **Marasmus**, which is characterized by extreme weight loss and muscle wasting due to insufficient calorie and protein intake.
 
• Protein-energy malnutrition is a broader term used to describe conditions like **Kwashiorkor** and **Marasmus**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Geographical Impact:**

 
 
• **Kwashiorkor** is prevalent in regions with **low socioeconomic conditions**, especially in parts of **Africa, South Asia**, and **Latin America** where food insecurity is widespread.
 
• Educational initiatives about balanced nutrition and access to resources are critical in combating this disease.
 
 
 
• **Prevention:**
 
 
• Ensuring a balanced diet rich in **proteins, carbohydrates, fats, and micronutrients** is essential for preventing malnutrition-related diseases.
 
• Government programs like the **Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS)** in India aim to address child malnutrition through supplementary nutrition and education.
 
 
 
• **Global Efforts:**
 
 
• Organizations like the **World Health Organization (WHO)** and **United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF)** work globally to combat malnutrition and promote food security.
 
• Programs such as **World Food Programme** provide food assistance in regions affected by famine and poverty.

questions.question: Who founded the Bahmani Kingdom?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Alauddin Bahman Shah**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Alauddin Bahman Shah** was the founder of the **Bahmani Kingdom**. He established this kingdom in **1347 AD**, marking the beginning of one of the most significant medieval dynasties in southern India.
 
• He was originally known as **Hasan Gangu**, a Brahmin convert to Islam, before adopting the title of **Alauddin Bahman Shah** when he ascended the throne.
 
• The Bahmani Kingdom was established as a response to the decline of the **Delhi Sultanate's control** over the Deccan region under **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**.
 
• **Gulbarga** was chosen as the initial capital of the Bahmani Kingdom, which later shifted to **Bidar**. The kingdom played a pivotal role in shaping the political and cultural history of the Deccan.
 
• The Bahmani Kingdom was the first independent Islamic state in southern India and served as a precursor to the later Deccan Sultanates.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Bahmani Kingdom:**
 
 
• The Bahmani Kingdom ruled parts of the Deccan region for nearly **200 years**, from **1347 AD to 1527 AD**.
 
• The kingdom was primarily located in present-day states of **Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Telangana**.
 
• The Bahmani rulers were known for their patronage of art, architecture, and literature, which significantly contributed to Deccan culture.
 
• One of their notable architectural achievements includes the construction of the **Gol Gumbaz** in Bijapur.
 
• The kingdom eventually disintegrated into five successor states, collectively known as the **Deccan Sultanates** (Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmednagar, Berar, and Bidar).
 
 
 
• **Important Characteristics of Other Options:**
 
 
• **Mir Zafar:** He was a Nawab of Bengal during the British era and played no role in the establishment of the Bahmani Kingdom.
 
• **Mohammad bin Tughlaq:** He was a ruler of the Delhi Sultanate, known for his ambitious projects and administrative failures, but he did not establish the Bahmani Kingdom.
 
• **Firoz Shah Bahmani:** He was a later ruler of the Bahmani dynasty but not its founder.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Bahmani Kingdom:**
 
 
• The Bahmani Kingdom was pivotal in fostering **Persian culture** and Islamic traditions in the Deccan region.
 
• The rulers maintained a strong rivalry with the **Vijayanagara Empire**, leading to frequent conflicts over the control of the Krishna-Tungabhadra region.
 
• The kingdom's eventual division into the Deccan Sultanates laid the groundwork for the political fragmentation of southern India before the arrival of the Mughals.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Timeline:** The Bahmani Kingdom was established in **1347 AD**, during the reign of **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**, marking a shift in power from Delhi to the Deccan.
 
• **Capital Shift:** The capital moved from **Gulbarga** to **Bidar**, signifying strategic and administrative changes.
 
• **Legacy:** The Bahmani Kingdom's cultural contributions, including advancements in architecture and literature, remain influential in the region.

• The movement was initiated in the **Bardoli taluka** of Gujarat against the **excessive tax hike of 22%** imposed by the colonial government.
 
• Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel earned the title of **"Sardar"** for his leadership and role in organizing the farmers during the Satyagraha.
 
• The farmers refused to pay the increased taxes and adopted the principle of **non-violent resistance**, inspired by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• The movement successfully forced the British authorities to roll back the tax hike, thus demonstrating the power of collective and peaceful resistance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Sardar Patel worked closely with **Mahatma Gandhi** and took charge of the Bardoli Satyagraha, where he organized farmers and led them in their protest.
 
• His title of **"Sardar"** (leader) was given by the women of Bardoli in recognition of his leadership skills and dedication to the cause.
 
• He played a critical role in maintaining discipline among the farmers and ensuring the movement adhered to the principles of **non-violence**.

• The British government had imposed a **22% hike in land revenue** in Bardoli, citing inflation, which severely burdened the farmers.
 
• The local farmers, suffering from poor harvests and economic hardships, found the tax hike unjustifiable and decided to protest.
 
 
 
• **Outcome of the Bardoli Satyagraha:**

• The success of the movement boosted the morale of Indians and demonstrated the effectiveness of **Satyagraha** as a tool for resistance.

• **Jawaharlal Nehru:** Later became the first Prime Minister of India and was a key figure in the independence movement, but he was not connected with this specific peasant uprising.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Bardoli Satyagraha:** It became a blueprint for future peasant movements in India, emphasizing **non-violence** and organization.
 
• **Sardar Patel's Role:** His leadership in Bardoli strengthened his position in the Indian National Congress and made him one of the most respected leaders of the time.

questions.question: Which of the following rivers is one of the three rivers whose interaction results in the formation of the Northern Plains?

__
 
• The **Brahmaputra River** is one of the three major rivers whose interaction leads to the formation of the **Northern Plains of India**. The other two rivers are the **Ganga** and the **Indus**.
 
• The **Northern Plains** are formed by the deposition of alluvium brought by the three major river systems—**Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra**—along with their tributaries.
 
• The **Brahmaputra River** originates from the **Angsi Glacier** in Tibet, where it is known as the **Yarlung Tsangpo**. It enters India through Arunachal Pradesh and flows through Assam.
 
• The river contributes significantly to the alluvial soil deposition across its flood plains, enriching the region's agricultural fertility, which is a key feature of the Northern Plains.
 
• The **interaction of these rivers** and their tributaries is responsible for creating one of the world's largest and most fertile plains, which supports extensive agriculture and sustains millions of livelihoods.

__

• The river is an important source of irrigation, transportation, and hydroelectric power in northeastern India.
 
• Major tributaries include **Subansiri, Manas, and Dibang.**
 
 
 
• **Northern Plains:**
 
 
• The **Northern Plains** are divided into three parts: the **Punjab Plains** (formed by the Indus river system), the **Ganga Plains**, and the **Brahmaputra Plains**.
 
• The plains are characterized by **fertile alluvial soil**, which supports agriculture as the primary economic activity.
 
• Crop cultivation includes **wheat, rice, sugarcane, and maize**, making the region the agricultural backbone of India.
 
• The plains also host major cities such as **Delhi, Kolkata, and Patna**, contributing to the socio-economic development of the country.
 
 
 
• **Other River Systems:**
 
 
• The **Indus River**, originating from Tibet, flows through India and Pakistan, contributing to the formation of the Punjab Plains.
 
• The **Ganga River**, originating from the **Gangotri Glacier**, flows through northern India and Bangladesh, forming the Ganga Plains.
 
• Both rivers, along with their tributaries, play a crucial role in shaping the geographical and cultural landscape of the region.
 
 
 
• **Importance of River Systems:**
 
 
• The interaction between the **Ganga, Brahmaputra, and Indus** river systems results in the **rejuvenation of soil fertility**, making the Northern Plains one of the most agriculturally productive regions in the world.
 
• These rivers support **economic activities** such as agriculture, fishing, and transportation, and provide water resources for domestic and industrial use.
 
• The plains formed by these rivers are densely populated due to their rich natural resources and favorable climate.

questions.question: The Government of India Act, _____ introduced dyarchy (a system of dual government) for the provinces of British India.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Government of India Act, 1919**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Government of India Act, 1919**, also known as the **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms**, introduced the system of **dyarchy** (dual government) in the provinces of British India.
 
• Dyarchy divided provincial subjects into two categories: **Transferred Subjects** and **Reserved Subjects**. Transferred subjects were administered by elected Indian ministers, while Reserved subjects remained under the control of British officials. 
 
• The Act aimed to provide a degree of **self-governance** to Indians while maintaining British control over key areas such as law and order, police, and finance. 
 
• The **Montagu Declaration** of 1917 had promised Indians greater self-governance, and the Government of India Act, 1919 was the legislative measure to fulfill that promise. 
 
• This Act was a step towards gradual constitutional development in India, but it was criticized for the limited scope of Indian representation and influence. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Government of India Act, 1909:**

 
 
• Also known as the **Morley-Minto Reforms**, this act introduced the concept of **separate electorates** for Muslims in India.
 
• It expanded the legislative councils and allowed Indians to be elected to legislative bodies, but its scope was limited. 
 
• The act aimed to incorporate Indians into governance but was criticized for dividing communities. 
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1858:**
 
 
• This Act was passed after the **Indian Rebellion of 1857** and marked the end of the East India Company's rule. 
 
• It transferred governance to the British Crown, establishing the office of the **Secretary of State for India** and the **Governor-General of India**.
 
• The act centralized administration but did not involve Indians in governance. 
 
 
 
• **Government of India Act, 1935:**
 
 
• This Act introduced **provincial autonomy** and proposed a federal structure for India, although the latter was not implemented. 
 
• It abolished dyarchy at the provincial level and expanded the electoral base. 
 
• The act also served as the basis for the Constitution of India, which was adopted in 1950. 
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Dyarchy:**
 
 
• Dyarchy involved the division of subjects into **Transferred** and **Reserved** categories.
 
• Transferred subjects included areas such as education, health, and agriculture, managed by Indian ministers. 
 
• Reserved subjects included law, order, and finance, controlled by British officials. 
 
• Dyarchy was criticized for its inefficiency and lack of real power for Indian ministers. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms:**

 
 
• These reforms were named after Edwin Montagu, the Secretary of State for India, and Lord Chelmsford, the Viceroy of India. 
 
• The reforms aimed to gradually introduce self-governance but faced criticism for their limited scope and failure to address demands for full independence. 
 
 
 
• **Impact of the 1919 Act:**
 
 
• The Act increased Indian representation in governance but maintained British control over key areas. 
 
• It led to the rise of nationalist movements demanding complete independence. 
 
 
 
• **Evolution of Indian Governance:**
 
 
• The Government of India Act, 1919 laid the foundation for subsequent constitutional developments, including the 1935 Act and the Indian Constitution. 
 
• It marked a shift from absolute British rule to limited Indian participation in governance.

__
 
• **Article 302** of the **Indian Constitution** empowers the **Parliament** to impose restrictions on **trade, commerce, and intercourse** between two states or within any part of Indian territory if it is in the **public interest**.
 
• This article plays a significant role in ensuring that trade and commerce do not disrupt public welfare, safety, or essential services.
 
• It provides the Parliament with the authority to regulate commerce, ensuring that specific regions or states do not face unequal or unfair trade practices.

• **Articles 301 to 307** are included in Part XIII and deal with the freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse.
 
• **Article 301:** Ensures the freedom of trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout the territory of India.
 
• **Article 302:** Empowers the Parliament to impose restrictions on this freedom in the interest of the public.

• While **Article 302** empowers the Parliament to impose restrictions on trade and commerce for public interest, **Article 304** empowers the **state legislatures** to impose restrictions within their respective states under specific conditions.
 
• Both articles aim to ensure that economic activities do not hinder public welfare or create inequalities.
 
 
 
• **Important Considerations:**
 
 
• Restrictions under Article 302 must align with the broader objectives of the Constitution, ensuring public welfare and equity.
 
• It safeguards against monopolistic practices or activities that could harm economic stability or fairness.

questions.question: Which of the following instruments is used to measure the heat absorbed or evolved?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Calorimeter**__.

__
 
• A **calorimeter** is an instrument used to measure the amount of heat absorbed or evolved during a physical or chemical process.
 
• The device works on the principle of heat transfer, where the heat exchanged between the system and its surroundings is quantified.
 
• It is commonly used in **thermodynamics, chemistry, and physics** for experiments involving heat measurement, such as combustion reactions and phase changes.
 
• **Types of calorimeters** include bomb calorimeters (used for measuring heat of combustion) and coffee cup calorimeters (used for simpler heat transfer experiments).
 
• Calorimeters are crucial for determining specific heat, enthalpy changes, and other thermodynamic properties of substances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Colorimeter**:
 
 
• A colorimeter measures the concentration of a solution by determining its color intensity.
 
• It is widely used in **biochemistry, water testing, and industrial applications** to analyze the concentration of substances.
 
• Colorimeters operate on the principle of Beer-Lambert's law, which relates the absorption of light to the concentration of the solution.
 
 
 
• **Ceilometer**:
 
 
• A ceilometer is a device used in meteorology to measure the height of cloud bases or the altitude of a cloud layer.
 
• It uses laser or light beams to determine cloud heights and is commonly employed at airports for weather observations.
 
• Modern ceilometers are capable of detecting multiple cloud layers simultaneously.
 
 
 
• **Clinometer**:
 
 
• A clinometer is an instrument used to measure angles of elevation or depression relative to gravity.
 
• It is utilized in **surveying, navigation, and construction** for determining slopes and angles.
 
• Clinometers are essential tools in geophysics and geology to study the tilt of geological formations.
 
 
 
• **Function of Calorimeters**:
 
 
• Calorimeters are used to measure **specific heat capacity**, latent heat, and enthalpy changes.
 
• They play a pivotal role in determining the calorific value of fuels and energy transfer in chemical reactions.
 
• For example, bomb calorimeters are used in food science to measure the energy content in food items.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Working Principle:**
 
 
• Calorimeters operate on the principle of conservation of energy, where no heat is lost to the surroundings during measurement.
 
• They are insulated to ensure accurate readings by preventing external heat exchange.
 
 
 
• **Applications:**
 
 
• Used in **chemical research** to study reaction enthalpies and combustion processes.
 
• In food science, calorimeters help determine the energy content of food products.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: Which of the following articles deals with the Right to Property?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 300A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 300A** of the **Indian Constitution** deals with the **Right to Property**. This article states that no person shall be deprived of their property except by the authority of law.
 
• The **Right to Property** was initially a fundamental right under **Article 19(1)(f)** and **Article 31**, but it was removed from the fundamental rights category by the **44th Amendment Act of 1978**.
 
• After the amendment, the Right to Property became a **legal right**, meaning it is no longer enforceable as a fundamental right but can be protected through legal remedies.
 
• This change was introduced to balance individual rights and the state's need to acquire land for public purposes, ensuring a fair legal process.
 
• **Article 300A** applies to the entire Indian territory and ensures that property can only be taken away through a legal process and adequate compensation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **History of Right to Property in India:**
 
 
• Initially, the **Right to Property** was a fundamental right under **Articles 19(1)(f)** and **31**. It guaranteed citizens the freedom to acquire, hold, and dispose of property.
 
• The **44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978**, shifted the Right to Property from fundamental rights to a constitutional legal right under **Article 300A**.
 
• This change was made to enable the government to acquire private property for public purposes without being challenged on fundamental rights grounds.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Article 300A:**
 
 
• It is a **constitutional legal right** enforceable through courts, but it does not hold the status of a fundamental right.
 
• Property can only be acquired by the state using a **legal process**, and fair compensation must be provided.
 
• Citizens can challenge unlawful confiscation of property under **Article 300A** in a court of law.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• Fundamental Rights such as those under **Articles 14-32** are protected against arbitrary state actions and can be enforced directly through the courts.
 
• Legal rights like **Article 300A** require legal procedures to be followed and do not offer direct protection against state actions unless challenged legally.
 
 
 
• **Examples of State Actions Related to Property:**
 
 
• Land acquisition for public infrastructure like highways, railways, and urban development projects is undertaken under laws like the **Land Acquisition Act, 2013**.
 
• The government ensures that property acquisition is done fairly and compensates owners adequately, aligning with **Article 300A**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The transition of the **Right to Property** from a fundamental right to a legal right reflects the government's intent to balance individual ownership rights with societal needs.
 
• The **44th Amendment Act** is a landmark amendment that significantly impacted land acquisition, urban planning, and infrastructure development processes in India.
 
• Citizens must understand their rights under **Article 300A** to ensure they receive adequate compensation if their property is acquired legally by the state.
